summary: Establishes initial Internet Code Point assignments for encoding IPv4 and IPv6 addresses inside Network Service Access Point (NSAP) addresses, and recommends an IANA assignment policy for the unassigned ICP values. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Different address systems need a short label showing which kind of address follows. This memo hands out the labels for internet addresses and sets rules for giving out the rest.

questions: what is an internet code point
how is an ipv6 address encoded in an nsap address
what icp value is used for ipv4
subtitle: Hands out the two code points that say whether an IPv4 or an IPv6 address is tucked inside an OSI NSAP address.

tldr.problem: OSI NSAP addresses can carry an Internet address, but the IPv6 assignment lived in a flawed section of RFC 1888 and the IPv4 assignment had never been formalized.
tldr.mechanism: Under AFI 35, which ITU-T gave to IANA, a 2-octet Internet Code Point of 0 means IPv6 and 1 means IPv4. The RFC defines the exact 20-octet layout for each and sets IETF consensus as the policy for ICP values 2 through 9999.
tldr.outcome: It replaces section 6 of RFC 1888, which had already been declared Historic by RFC 4048, and it updates both of those RFCs.

facts.label: AFI assigned to IANA for binary encoding

today: RFC 4548 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 1888 and RFC 4048, and no later RFC is listed as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
Section 6 of RFC 1888 gave the Internet Code Point (ICP) value 0 to the encoding of an IPv6 address in a Network Service Access Point (NSAP) address. It also defined ways to encode an NSAP address in an IPv6 address. Those encodings came with many warnings and limits, appear never to have been used in any IPv6 deployment, and section 6 contained minor errors. RFC 4048 then obsoleted RFC 1888 and declared it Historic.

The authors believe the errors came partly from the ITU-T specification X.213, which gave Authority and Format Identifier (AFI) 35 to IANA but was not freely publicized or explained in an RFC. This document supplies that explanation, corrects section 6 because other documents still refer to it, and formalizes an ICP for IPv4, which no earlier RFC had done.
sections.plainLanguage: An old rulebook had mistakes and nobody could easily read the original rules behind it. This memo writes the rules down clearly and fixes the mistakes.

sections.title: How an NSAP Address Is Built
sections.content:
An NSAP address (NSAPA) is 20 octets long. It has an Initial Domain Part (IDP) and a Domain Specific Part (DSP). The IDP is an Authority and Format Identifier (AFI), one binary octet, followed by an Initial Domain Identifier (IDI). The IDI is a four-digit decimal number stored in two octets as Binary Coded Decimal, one digit per nibble, using the binary values 0000 through 1001.

ITU-T X.213 allocated two AFIs to IANA. AFI 34 is for NSAPs in Decimal Numeric Format, and this document does not address it because it is unclear what use, if any, can be made of it. AFI 35 is used for binary encoding. For AFI 35 the IDI holds an ICP, which because of the decimal encoding must be between 0 and 9999. The DSP is the remaining 17 octets, in a format defined by IANA or by another party with IANA consent.
sections.plainLanguage: An NSAP address is like a long code with a front part that says what kind of code it is and a back part that holds the details. The front part uses a small number, called the code point, to say what is inside.

sections.title: The ICP Assignments and Policy
sections.content:
X.213 assumed ICP 0 for IPv6 and assumed IANA would assign an ICP for IPv4, with 1 expected. This document records IANA's assignments: ICP 0 is IPv6, defined in section 3.2, and ICP 1 is IPv4, defined in section 3.1.

The remaining decimal values 2 through 9999 MUST be assigned on an IETF consensus basis. IANA SHOULD NOT assign an ICP unless a corresponding format is defined and published at the time of assignment.
sections.plainLanguage: Two labels are already taken: 0 for the newer kind of internet address and 1 for the older kind. Anyone who wants another label has to get the community to agree first, and must have written down what it means.

sections.title: IPv4 Address in an NSAP Address
sections.content:
If an IPv4 address has to be embedded in a 20-octet NSAP address, this format MUST be used. The AFI is 35 and the ICP is 1. The 4-octet IPv4 address sits in the first 4 octets of the DSP. The last 13 octets of the DSP are not specified here; they MUST be present, have no intrinsic significance for IPv4, and default to zero.

To get the IPv4 address back, strip the first 3 and last 13 octets. If the NSAP contents are passed to a higher layer, the last 13 octets SHOULD be passed too. When such an address is used for routing in an IPv4 routing architecture, only the 4-octet IPv4 address MAY be considered. The RFC suggests expressing an IP address in the ATM Forum address format, or routing CLNP packets that encapsulate IPv4 using several leading octets of the IPv4 address as a CLNP routing prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv4 address goes in the first slot of the details area, and the rest of the space is filled with zeros. To read the address, you just cut off the front label and the empty padding.

sections.title: IPv6 Address in an NSAP Address
sections.content:
If an IPv6 address has to be embedded in a 20-octet NSAP address, this format MUST be used. The AFI is 35 and the ICP is 0. The 16-octet IPv6 address fills the first 16 octets of the DSP. The last DSP octet is a selector. It MUST be present but has no intrinsic significance for IPv6. Its default value is zero, but other values may be used as specified for a specific application. As an example, it may specify one of 255 possible port numbers.

To get the IPv6 address back, strip the first 3 octets and the 20th octet. If the contents are passed to a higher layer, the last octet SHOULD be passed as well. For routing in an IPv6 routing architecture, only the 16-octet IPv6 address MAY be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: The long IPv6 address goes into the details area with one spare slot at the end. That slot is normally zero but can carry a small extra number if an application wants one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the NSAP encoding of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses is compatible with the corresponding security mechanisms of RFC 4301, so the document introduces no new security exposure in the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting an address inside this wrapper does not open any new doors for trouble, because it works with the existing security rules.
